concept.title: Authenticating API requests
concept.shortdesc: Authenticate every CorgiBase API request with Basic authentication or an OAuth 2.0 access token. Use HTTPS and keep credentials out of client-side code.

conbody.p: Both methods identify the integration and its allowed scopes. Choose the method your integration supports; for most server-side integrations, an API key is the simplest option. Send credentials only in the Authorization header, never in a URL.

section.title: Basic authentication
section.p: Use an API key as the Basic authentication username and leave the password empty. Your HTTP client encodes the credentials and sends them in the Authorization header. For example, with curl:

Create and manage keys in under SettingsAPI keys. Choose only the scopes the integration needs, and use a sandbox key while developing. Basic authentication sends the key with each request, so store it in a secrets manager and use it only from a trusted server.

section.title: OAuth 2.0 client credentials
section.p: For a server-to-server integration that needs short-lived credentials, use the OAuth 2.0 client credentials grant. Register an integration to obtain a client ID and client secret, and request only the scopes it needs. Exchange the credentials for an access token, then send that token as a bearer token on API requests:
The token response includes an access token and its lifetime. Use the token until it expires, then request another; do not send the client secret with API requests.

Keep the client secret on your server and out of source control, browser code, and mobile apps. Use a separate client for each integration so you can rotate its secret without disrupting other clients.

section.title: Choosing a method
section.p: Use Basic authentication with an API key when you want a straightforward integration using the scopes and live or sandbox access configured for that key. Use OAuth 2.0 when your server can securely store a client secret and benefit from access tokens that expire. Never share credentials between unrelated integrations; revoke or rotate credentials that may have been exposed.
